title: Why REST APIs Are Used
subtopics: Integrating mobile apps and external platforms
learning_outcomes: Explain how why rest apis are used affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from connecting frontend and backend applications to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on why rest apis are used in introduction to rest api development. You will connect connecting frontend and backend applications to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Why REST APIs Are Used matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying connecting frontend and backend applications deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: An API contract describes what a consumer may ask for and what the provider promises to return. In this lesson, treat “Why REST APIs Are Used” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.expected_output: A consumer can identify the target resource and requested operation from a documented contract; no implementation language is implied.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Connecting frontend and backend applications”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Sharing data between services” and “Supporting independent application development”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Start with the problem and the consumer contract before choosing tools. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating why rest apis are used. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “Connecting frontend and backend applications” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for Why REST APIs Are Used with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating why rest apis are used as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: An API contract describes what a consumer may ask for and what the provider promises to return. In this lesson, treat “Why REST APIs Are Used” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.
Next, connect this idea to Lesson 6: Real-World Applications of REST APIs.
